budget_cents.description: What the trip is MEANT to cost, integer minor units, denominated in `currency`. Finance keeps every actual cent and already tags postings with an axon-trip-id; the intention had no home at all, so the two halves of "did I overspend" were an HTTP call apart and never compared.

currency.description: ISO 4217, e.g. EUR. Load-bearing twice: it denominates `budget_cents`, and a retrospective may not record a cost against a plan that carries none, because a number with no unit is not a cost.

retrospective.description: The plan's close-out record, or null. Exactly the three fields PRD 8.2 rules. Top-level rather than nested because the served object is flat.

external_id.description: Idempotency key together with (plan_id, item_type): writing the same external_id twice updates the row rather than duplicating it. Producers namespace it by source (`scouting:<id>`, `calendar:<entry-id>`) or reuse the provider's own id for a journey or place. An outcome uses `outcome:<stage-id>`, so re-recording one stage corrects it rather than adding a second.

transportPayload.description: A selected transport option held in the itinerary. This is the item to write for 'hold this connection in the plan'. Provider fields beyond those named here are preserved.

journey.description: The provider's journey record. Its `id` is what a stage's selected_option_id refers to, so it should be the same string used as the item's external_id.

bookingPayload.description: What makes a stage's `booked` status mean something. Before this, `booked` was a string the API accepted with nothing behind it: no order reference, no fare name, no refundability, no cancellation deadline. Axon never buys anything, so a booking record is always evidence of a purchase made elsewhere, entered by hand or parsed from a confirmation.

provider.description: Who sold it. `bahn.de`, an airline, an agency.

order_ref.description: The provider's own reference: an order number, PNR or booking code. Together with the provider this is what lets you find the booking again on their side.

fare_name.description: The fare as the provider names it — Sparpreis, Flexpreis, a fare class. Kept verbatim rather than normalised, because the name is what the conditions attach to.

free_cancellation_until.description: The last moment cancelling is free, as a date or datetime. This is the one field with a deadline attached, and calendar turns it into a `deadline` entry.

amount_cents.description: Integer minor units. A price in floating point is a price that eventually disagrees with the receipt.

ticket_file_ref.description: A reference to the ticket file, never the file. Where it lives is a deployment fact and belongs in the private overlay.

traveler_name_present.description: Whether the ticket is name-bound, as a boolean. Deliberately not the name: whose name is on a ticket is personal data this repository has no reason to hold, and knowing that a ticket is non-transferable is the part a plan needs.

stage_id.description: The `id` of the stage this price belongs to, when it is known. Optional: nothing produces one yet, so this makes attribution possible going forward and retrofits nothing. A stage id is NOT durable -- generated_stages mints ids from the sequence and remints them on a real route change -- so a consumer treats a missing match as unattributed rather than as an error.

stayPayload.description: Where you sleep, next to how you get there. Written from an accommodation search result (the item's title carries the property name, external_id namespaces the provider's own id, e.g. `booking.com:1234567`). Coordinates are required because the place matching downstream runs on them; provider fields beyond those named here are preserved.

provider.description: Where the result came from. `booking.com`, an agency, a direct website.

url.description: The provider's page for this stay, so the plan holds a bookable link rather than a name to re-search.

amount_cents.description: Total for the whole stay, integer minor units. A price in floating point is a price that eventually disagrees with the receipt.

rating.description: As the provider scores it, kept verbatim on the provider's own scale.

stage_id.description: The `id` of the stage this price belongs to, when it is known. Optional: nothing produces one yet, so this makes attribution possible going forward and retrofits nothing. A stage id is NOT durable -- generated_stages mints ids from the sequence and remints them on a real route change -- so a consumer treats a missing match as unattributed rather than as an error.

booked.description: True once the stay is actually booked. A stay copied from a search result is a candidate, and trips' cost roll-up counts its price as booked only when this is true or `order_ref` is set.

order_ref.description: The provider's booking reference, once booked. Its presence also marks the stay as booked.

optionSetPayload.description: Every option one search offered, including the ones not taken. Recorded because a fare that was not chosen cannot be queried back later at yesterday's price: an unrecorded option set is gone, not merely unwritten.

from.description: The origin as one string (a place name, or an IATA code for a flight search).

to.description: The single destination a search asked about. A multi-destination plan search writes the declared literal "(multiple)" here and puts every place in destinations[]; the literal is declared so it is not a magic value invented at a call site.

destinations.description: Every destination a multi-destination search ranked. Absent for a single-destination option set.

budget_cents.description: What the search was told to stay under, in integer minor units.

total_price.description: The older float form, in units of `currency`. tools/sparpreis-watch writes it every 12 hours (capabilities/sparpreis-watch/service.toml) and rows in that shape already exist; plan search writes estimated_cost_cents in integer minor units instead. A reader has to accept both.

estimated_cost_cents.description: What this option was expected to cost, in integer minor units of `currency`. Null when no fare source could price it.

window.description: The feasible window this option was priced for. Dates and a calendar verdict only: no calendar entry title crosses this boundary.

factors.description: The visible reasons behind `score`. Same shape as the feed evaluator's factors (capabilities/comms/src/evaluation.rs); weights sum to 1 across the factors that could be measured.

observed_at.description: When these fares were seen. A stored price with no observation time cannot be told apart from a current one.

revision.description: The scoring revision that produced these scores (capabilities/trips/src/plan_search.rs, PLAN_SEARCH_REVISION). Two option sets are comparable only at the same revision. Optional, not required: the plan-search writer always sets it, and the option_set rows that predate it -- every one tools/sparpreis-watch has written -- carry none.

degraded.description: Every input the search could not measure. A score computed with a factor missing is comparable inside one option set and not across two with different degraded sets.

retrospectivePayload.description: One retrospective per plan, written by POST /api/plans/{id}/retrospective. Exactly three fields, ruled and closed by PRD 8.2: what it cost, would I do it again, what would I change. Deliberately different from the `outcome` item, which measures one stage against the option it was chosen under -- per-stage measurement against per-plan judgement.

cost_cents.description: Integer minor units, denominated in the PLAN's `currency`. The retrospective carries no currency of its own, so the money is named exactly once and a second field cannot disagree with it.

currency.description: Echoed from the plan for the reader's convenience; never stored on the retrospective row.

again.description: Would I do this trip again. A closed vocabulary, and the database enforces it with a CHECK -- one of the two reasons this is a table rather than a JSON payload.

change_note.description: What I would change, in the traveller's own words. An only-copy human sentence, which is why the vault projection carries it verbatim (Principle 8).
